content.title: Read the Diff and the History
content.hook: When a file looks wrong, your first instinct might be to stare at the current version.
content.context:
A better question is:

> “What changed?”

Git can show you the difference.

A simplified diff might look like this:

```diff
-const total = price * quantity;
+const total = price + quantity;
```

One line changed.

That single difference is a much stronger debugging clue than “the cart total is weird.”
goals: Use diffs and history to reconstruct what changed and why a project moved from one state to another.

content.question: Which line most likely explains the broken total?

options.text: Neither line; Git does not show meaningful evidence.

feedback.correct: The added line changes the operation. The diff tells you exactly what changed between versions.
feedback.incorrect: The added line changes the operation. The diff tells you exactly what changed between versions.

content.title: Read history
content.text:
A project history can be viewed with:

```bash
git log
```

A simplified history might show:

```text
7a1 Fix cart total
5bd Add cart quantity control
2c4 Build cart summary
```

Now you can ask:

> “Which change introduced the behavior I am investigating?”

content.question:
A feature worked yesterday.

Today it is broken.

History shows:

```text
A  Build feature
B  Add loading state
C  Refactor total calculation
```

The bug first appears after C.

What is the best next move?

options.text: Blame every file in the project.
Assume A is broken because it is older.

feedback.correct: Start with the earliest known point where the behavior became wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the earliest known point where the behavior became wrong.

content.title: Compare before guessing
content.text:
The engineering loop is:

```text
symptom
  ↓
find last known good state
  ↓
compare changes
  ↓
form a hypothesis
  ↓
test the hypothesis
```

That is the same reasoning skill you learned in the earlier debugging curriculum, now applied to project history.

content.question:
Which tool answers which question?

1. “What changed in my files?”
2. “What commits exist?”
3. “Which exact commit might contain the regression?”

options.text: `git diff` → `git log` → compare history and inspect the relevant commit

feedback.correct: Use each command as a question, then combine the answers into an investigation.
feedback.incorrect: Use each command as a question, then combine the answers into an investigation.
